opus-5.5.text:
I think it's important to be precise about this, because there's a lot of excitement and sometimes the story gets told as if AlphaFold solved drug discovery. It didn't, and it was never meant to. What it did was remove one very specific, very significant bottleneck: knowing the three-dimensional structure of a protein.

For decades, if you wanted to know what a protein looked like, you had to go through X-ray crystallography, cryo-EM, or NMR. That could take a PhD student years, sometimes with no result at all, and it was expensive. So structural information was scarce. Before AlphaFold we had experimental structures for a fraction of known proteins. With the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database, working with EMBL-EBI, we released predicted structures for over 200 million proteins, essentially everything catalogued in UniProt. That changed the starting point for a lot of researchers. Instead of asking "can we get a structure?", they could ask "what do we do with this structure?"

Where does that matter for drug discovery? Early in the pipeline: target identification, understanding the mechanism of a disease, figuring out where a small molecule might bind, thinking about which proteins might be druggable. Structure gives you a hypothesis much faster. We've seen it used across neglected diseases, antibiotic resistance, enzyme design, and by large numbers of researchers in low-resource settings who never had access to crystallography facilities.

But we should be honest about the rest of the pipeline. Most of the cost and time in drug discovery goes into later stages, clinical trials, safety, efficacy in actual humans, and a lot of drugs fail there for reasons structure alone can't tell you. Proteins are also dynamic; they move, they interact with other molecules, and a static prediction is only part of the picture. That's why later work, like AlphaFold 3, focuses on modelling interactions between proteins, DNA, RNA, ligands, and why efforts like Isomorphic Labs are trying to build on that to tackle more of the chemistry and design side.

So my assessment is: AlphaFold accelerated the science that sits underneath drug discovery, and it democratized access to structural biology in a way that's genuinely changed how people work. But it's one piece. The bigger lesson for me is that AI can collapse a problem that was thought to take decades into something you can query in seconds, and the question now is which other bottlenecks in biology are amenable to that same kind of breakthrough.

r001.rationale: It identifies knowing a protein’s 3D structure as a major bottleneck and says AlphaFold made structural information available much faster for early drug-discovery work.

r002.rationale: It says much of drug discovery’s cost and time remains in later stages, including clinical trials and testing safety and efficacy in humans, which structure predictions cannot resolve.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think it's important to be honest about what AlphaFold did and didn't do. Drug discovery has many bottlenecks, and structure was one of them, but it was never the only one, and I'd argue it wasn't even the hardest one.

What AlphaFold changed is that, for most proteins, you no longer have to spend months or years, and sometimes a PhD's worth of effort, trying to crystallize something before you can even start reasoning about it structurally. That used to be a gate. Many targets in the human proteome simply had no experimental structure, and now there's a reasonable starting point for essentially all of them. So the first bottleneck, "can I see what I'm working with," has largely been removed. That's real, and we've seen it in how quickly the database was adopted. Millions of researchers using it isn't a vanity metric to me; it tells you the gate was actually blocking people.

But then you run into the next set of problems, and these are the ones I find more interesting. A static structure of a protein on its own doesn't tell you how it interacts with a small molecule, how it moves, what happens when it's in a complex with other proteins, or what a mutation does to its function. That's part of why we pushed toward AlphaFold 3 and modeling interactions across ligands, nucleic acids, and ions, because the question drug developers actually care about is "does this molecule bind here and what does it do," not "what does this protein look like in isolation."

And then there's everything downstream of structure: is this target even causally relevant to the disease, will the compound be toxic, will it be absorbed, will it survive a clinical trial. Those are where most drug programs fail, and they're not structural questions. So I'd put it this way. AlphaFold took a problem that was a decades-long bottleneck and made it mostly a solved input. That shifts where the hard work is rather than eliminating it. If anything, it exposed how much of the remaining difficulty is in biology and chemistry we still don't understand well enough to model, and that's what we're working on now, at Isomorphic and in the research group.

r001.rationale: The response calls protein structure a drug-discovery bottleneck and says AlphaFold largely removed the delay of obtaining structures, which could take months or years.

r002.rationale: It says most drug programs fail downstream and explicitly includes whether a compound will survive a clinical trial among the remaining challenges.

astra-6.text:
I think AlphaFold has made a very important contribution, but we should distinguish understanding a protein’s structure from discovering a drug. Drug discovery has many bottlenecks, and AlphaFold helps with one of them: getting a structural picture of the biological machinery you want to understand or intervene in.

That gives researchers a starting point for asking better questions. How might this protein work? Where might a molecule bind? What experiments should we do next? Having a predicted structure can help them move more quickly from a hypothesis to an experiment.

But a structure doesn’t tell you everything. Proteins move, they interact with other molecules, and what happens in a cell is much more complex than a single structural model. You still need to establish that acting on a particular target will help treat a disease, and that a candidate drug is effective and safe.

So I see AlphaFold as an enabling technology. It can reduce uncertainty and accelerate parts of the research process, but it doesn’t remove the need for experiments or solve drug discovery on its own.

r001.rationale: It identifies getting a structural picture of the target as one of drug discovery’s bottlenecks and says AlphaFold can help researchers move more quickly from hypotheses to experiments.

r002.rationale: It says researchers still need to establish treatment benefit, effectiveness, and safety, but does not state that clinical validation remains a bottleneck.

sol-6.1.text:
I think AlphaFold has made a very important contribution, but it’s useful to distinguish understanding a biological system from developing a medicine. Knowing the structure of a protein can help researchers understand how it works, what might go wrong in disease, and where they might intervene. AlphaFold makes that structural information much more accessible, so scientists can explore hypotheses that previously might have taken a great deal of time and effort to investigate.

But structure is only one part of drug discovery. You still need to establish that a target matters for the disease, find a molecule that affects it in the right way, and demonstrate that the molecule is safe and effective. Proteins also move and interact with other molecules; a predicted structure doesn’t capture all of that biology.

So I would describe AlphaFold as a powerful enabling technology. It can remove a significant barrier to understanding and accelerate parts of the discovery process, while experiments and clinical validation remain essential.

r001.rationale: It says AlphaFold makes protein structural information more accessible and speeds work that previously could take substantial time and effort, identifying structure determination as a barrier it helps overcome.

r002.rationale: It says clinical validation remains essential, but does not characterize it as a drug-discovery bottleneck.
